chunks: A number of our companions, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from Ali ibn al-Hakam, from Muhammad ibn Yahya, from Abu Baseer, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), who said:

I asked him (peace be upon him) about a woman who fell ill during the month of Ramadan and died in Shawwal, so she bequeathed to me that I make up the fasts on her behalf. He (peace be upon him) said: 'Was she cured from her illness?' I said: 'No, she died in it.' He (peace be upon him) said: 'Do not make up the fasts on her behalf, for Allah, Mighty and Majestic, did not make it obligatory upon her.' I said: 'But I desire to make up the fasts on her behalf, and she had bequeathed that to me.' He (peace be upon him) said: 'How can you make up for something which Allah did not make obligatory upon her? So, if you desire to fast for yourself, then fast.'

key_terms.لَمْ يَجْعَلْهُ عَلَيْهَا: Did not make it obligatory upon her

ai.seo_question: What is the ruling on making up missed fasts for a woman who died while still ill in Ramadan?
ai.summary: This hadith clarifies the distinction between obligatory and voluntary fasting by ruling that a woman who dies while still ill in Ramadan is exempt from qada, as the obligation was not fixed upon her. It highlights the Shia principle that one may fast voluntarily on behalf of the deceased even if not strictly required, reflecting the flexibility in devotional acts. This ruling underscores the theological view that divine obligations are contingent upon capacity and cure, rather than mere time passage.
